topic: Periodic Trends Across Periods and Down Groups
title: Periodic Trends on One Map Explained Simply | PUC Chemistry Class 11
description:
Sodium is stored under kerosene, chlorine cleans drinking water, and neon glows in a sign but almost never reacts. Three very different personalities, and one map predicts all three. In this animated lesson for PUC and Class 11 Chemistry (NCERT Chapter 3, Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties) we put every periodic trend together on one live periodic table.

You will see why size and nuclear pull drive almost everything: across a period the nucleus gains protons while electrons fill the same shell, and down a group a new shell is added each time. Then a live periodic table shades and draws arrows for five trends, one at a time: atomic radius (Li 152 pm to F 64 pm, Cs 262 pm), ionization enthalpy (Li 520 to Ne 2081 kJ/mol), electron gain enthalpy, electronegativity (F 4.0) and metallic character. We explain why the two ends of a period react the most, prove with water that Na2O is basic and Cl2O7 is acidic (with a live balance counter and litmus), and walk the period 3 oxides from basic through amphoteric Al2O3 to acidic, plus the neutral oxides CO, NO and N2O. Then the exam trap, an original NEET pattern question with a full solution, a recap card and three questions to check yourself.

This is Episode 36 of our PUC Chemistry series.

Made for PUC (Karnataka), CBSE Class 11, NEET and JEE Main students.

In this video:
0:00 Three elements, one map
0:32 What is a periodic trend?
1:00 The live periodic table: five trends
2:08 Pause and think: potassium or magnesium?
2:22 Why the two ends react the most
3:14 Worked example: Na2O and Cl2O7 with water
3:56 Oxides across period 3
4:23 Exam trap: does radius grow across a period?
4:48 Practice question (NEET pattern)
5:24 Recap and three questions to answer

Next episode: Exceptions and Anomalous Periodic Behaviour. Why does boron break the ionization enthalpy trend, and why does chlorine beat fluorine?
